Project: YCompany eClaims | Version 1.0 | Author: Utsav Verma (Senior Staff Engineer, Nagarro) | Date: 07-Jul-2026 | Classification: Confidential

Layer 1 — Client / Edge
Web · Staff · Partner Portals

Layer 2 — API Gateway / Ingress

Layer 4 — Async / Messaging
EventBridge · SQS · SNS · Lambda
Shared by several workflows — the label names them, e.g. ①②③

Notes & Conventions:
1. All external traffic is HTTPS / TLS 1.2+. Every API request carries an OAuth2 JWT (15-min access / 7-day refresh) issued by the Auth Service; each service checks the signature itself with the Auth Service's signing keys, cached locally, so no request waits on a call to the Auth Service.
2. Photos and PDFs go straight from the browser to S3 with pre-signed URLs; the Document Service only issues the URL and registers the metadata and SHA-256 digest.
3. Every status change publishes a domain event. SQS delivers it to the Notification Service (SMS through SNS, email through SES); change-data capture copies claim data to Redshift, where reports run as background jobs.
4. Layer 6 services are cross-cutting and govern every layer above — shown by representative dashed flows (KMS → data at rest, audit trail → S3 Object Lock, Okta → Auth Service). Every business action is also written to the hash-chained application audit trail.
5. Solid arrows = request / data flow (protocol or event labelled); dashed arrows = cross-cutting / governance / association. The Policy Administration System is an open item (E3, page 1), drawn in the to-be-confirmed style.

Why no managed API Gateway? Classic API-Gateway capabilities are already delivered by existing components (verified against the SAD):
Routing / dispatch → ALB (Multi-AZ, path routes /auth /claims /documents /workshops /payments /reports)   |   AuthN / AuthZ → Auth Service (OAuth2/JWT) + RBAC + Okta SSO, ALB OIDC offload
Rate limiting / throttling → AWS WAF + Shield (edge rate-based rules)   |   Caching → CloudFront (edge) + ElastiCache Redis (data, <100 ms)
Canary / blue-green → CodePipeline + CodeDeploy, ALB weighted target groups   |   Circuit breaker / retries → service-level breakers + exponential backoff
Distributed tracing → CloudWatch + X-Ray   |   Request validation → in-service (FastAPI + Pydantic)
A managed API Gateway would only add per-API-key usage plans / metering — not required, since partners integrate via the Partner Portal, not raw metered APIs.

Notes & Conventions:
1. Route 53 (G1) is the network entry point — DNS resolution for every internet-facing request (SAD §4 Layer 2) — and the Region switch: CloudFront's origin hostname is a G1 failover record whose health checks follow the G4 routing controls (Note 15).
2. Every AWS component on this page and the CI/CD page uses real AWS Architecture Icons and proper AWS group containers (VPC/AZ/Subnet/Security-Group) — a departure from pages 1-4's plain colour-block convention, scoped to these two infrastructure pages only.
3. Phase 1 = two AWS Regions, each Multi-AZ (3 zones): us-east-1 (N. Virginia) is primary and serves all traffic; us-east-2 (Ohio) is a warm standby at minimum capacity. Multi-Region active-active remains out of scope (§10).
4. This page is the deployment-topology companion to page 4 — page 4 names every AWS service per logical layer; this page places the same services on a physical VPC/AZ/subnet network map.
5. V1–V6 are tagged once in us-east-1 and V1′–V6′ once in us-east-2, to avoid clutter; the other zones repeat the pattern untagged. us-east-1c's data subnet is deliberately sparser — RDS/ElastiCache Multi-AZ is a standard 2-AZ pair; only the 3-node OpenSearch domain needs a third zone for write quorum.
6. The Data Subnet reuses the Private Subnet's group-container styling — AWS's icon set has no distinct "isolated subnet" container; isolation is conveyed by the label, not a different icon.
7. Where two connectors cross, the crossing is drawn as an arc jump; no two connectors share a parallel route.
8. The Auth Service is grouped under Layer 2 in SAD §4 for its logical capability, but physically runs as an ECS Fargate task in the private/app subnet alongside every other microservice.
9. Every component sits behind a Security Group; one is drawn illustratively around the us-east-1a Fargate icon rather than repeated on every instance.
10. AWS SNS and SES appear twice by design: N4 is the internal EventBridge-driven pub/sub; D3/D4 represent the last-mile hop out to the carrier/mail server — two different network hops through the same managed service, not a duplicate.
11. CI/CD (CodePipeline/CodeBuild/CodeDeploy/ECR, SAD §4 Layer 6/§8) has its own dedicated page (tab 6) rather than being drawn here — it's a deployment-time concern, not a runtime network path.
12. E3 (Policy Administration System) is carried through from page 1 in the same to-be-confirmed styling — this page does not resolve that open item, only shows where its traffic would enter.
13. On-diagram captions are short names only; full descriptions, zone-specific variants and protocol detail are in the registry table above, indexed by the same G/V/N/D/E tags used on the diagram.
14. External SaaS is a right-side column adjacent to us-east-1c and sourced from that zone's NAT Gateway (V2) for short, direct routing — egress is identical from any zone's NAT Gateway (us-east-1a/1b not drawn). After failover, us-east-2's NAT Gateways (V2′) egress to the same providers (not drawn).
15. Failover (warm standby): on a us-east-1 outage the on-call runs the pre-approved runbook — promote the V4′ replica, promote N7′ and point it at V4′, pre-scale V3′, then flip the G4 routing controls (us-east-2 On, us-east-1 Off) so Route 53 answers with V1′. CloudWatch alarms page the on-call but never move traffic, and a recovered us-east-1 cannot take traffic back while its control is Off. Failback is the same runbook in reverse, after re-seeding us-east-1.
16. Replication and targets: RDS cross-Region read replica (V4 → V4′), OpenSearch cross-cluster replication over inter-Region VPC peering (V6 → V6′), S3 Cross-Region Replication (N1 → N1′) and Secrets Manager replica secrets (N7 → N7′). ElastiCache is not replicated and starts cold; Redshift recovers from a cross-Region snapshot copy; EventBridge, SQS, SNS, Lambda and Step Functions run in both Regions (Terraform), and messages queued in us-east-1 are not replicated. Region failure: RTO < 30 min; RPO < 5 min for the database and < 15 min for S3 objects. AZ failure: RTO < 15 min, RPO < 5 min.
17. Held ready in us-east-2: SES production access, SNS SMS registration, partner and Policy Admin allow-lists for the V2′ addresses, ACM certificates for V1′ and raised Fargate quotas.
18. Zone names (us-east-1a …) map to different physical zones in each AWS account; Terraform pins the zone IDs (use1-az…), so the names here are illustrative.
19. V1 and V1′ are drawn as one band per Region because an ALB is a single regional resource with a node in each zone's public subnet; the arrows from each band are its target group reaching the Fargate tasks in every zone.

Notes & Conventions:
1. Reading order: Source (P1) → CodePipeline (P2) orchestrates three sequential stages via a shared S3 artifact bucket (P3) — Stage 1 Build (P4→P5), Stage 2 Infrastructure (P6, Terraform, manual approval gate), Stage 3 Deploy (P7, blue/green).
2. Cost framing: CodePipeline charges a small flat fee per active pipeline with no idle-time charge; CodeBuild bills only actual build-minutes — no idle build server to provision, patch or scale. Materially cheaper than a self-managed Jenkins controller running around the clock, and avoids a second CI/CD tool alongside AWS's own managed equivalents.
3. Blue/Green mechanism: Blue = current/live (P10), Green = new candidate (P11); CodeDeploy (P7) shifts ALB weighted-target-group traffic (P8) — the mechanism behind SAD §7's "blue-green deployment for zero-downtime releases."
4. Rollback: A CloudWatch (R1) alarm on ECS/ALB health during the traffic shift triggers automated traffic-back-to-Blue and Green deregistration — ties to §7's Resilience/Reliability row.
5. CodeBuild appears twice (P4, P6) — two distinct projects (app build/test, Terraform plan/apply), one managed service; mirrors the Cloud/Deployment page's own SNS/SES dual-appearance note.
6. CloudWatch (R1) and Secrets Manager/KMS/IAM (Q1-Q3) also appear on the Cloud/Deployment page (N7-N10) — same services, two different lifecycle moments (steady-state runtime there, deployment-time here), not a duplicate.
7. This page is a companion to the Cloud/Deployment page — it does not redraw the VPC/AZ/subnet topology. The ECS Service/task-set icons here stand in for the same Multi-AZ Fargate runtime (V3 there); the ALB (P8) is the same regional ALB (V1 there), not a second load balancer; us-east-2's V1′/V3′ receive the same release through P13.
8. Q3 (IAM) is shown with no drawn edge, consistent with the Cloud/Deployment page's N9 — its role relationship applies uniformly to every pipeline stage.
9. Source Repository (P1) is rendered in the same to-be-confirmed/assumption style as the Policy Administration System (E3) on pages 1 and 5 — no source-control platform is named anywhere in the case study or SAD.
10. Multi-Region release: ECR replicates every image to us-east-2 (P12); Terraform (P6) applies the us-east-1 and us-east-2 stacks; after the us-east-1 deploy succeeds, a cross-Region CodeDeploy action (P13) runs the same blue/green into the us-east-2 warm-standby service, so both Regions run the same image. The pipeline and Terraform state live in us-east-1, so releases pause during a us-east-1 outage.
